title: Syllabus
text:
CPSC 221 teaches you to design, implement, and analyze the classic data structures and algorithms of computer science — and to reason rigorously about when and why to use them. You’ll come away able to:

Define and articulate the functionality of classic data structures such as stacks, queues, dictionaries, and priority queues by their Abstract Data Type (ADT).
Design algorithms and structures to implement novel ADTs based on properties of the data and intended use.
Implement classic and novel data structures in modern C++, including arrays, linked lists, AVL trees, and hash tables.
Analyze the efficiency (time and space) of algorithms and data structures using asymptotic notation.
Justify algorithmic choices using iterative and recursive proofs of correctness.
Evaluate asymptotic time and space tradeoffs between implementation options.
Identify the structures and algorithms necessary for solving complex problems.
Synthesize and apply algorithmic and analytical design choices to form complete software solutions to classic problems.

You must pass an appropriately weighted average of the examlets and final exam in order to pass the course.
Programming assignments and homework are project-like: you (and an optional partner) manage your own progress within a 1–2 week work window, and assignments may overlap. Labs are weekly coding exercises auto-graded on PrairieLearn; your 8 highest lab scores (of 10) count toward your grade. Examlets are (nearly) weekly, self-scheduled, and focus on the previous week’s content — practice material includes old exams and PrairieLearn practice problems.

Collaboration policy
Some assignments allow groups of up to 2; others require independent work. For homework and most programming assignments, you may work with at most one partner — but each student must submit their own copy, even if it’s identical to their partner’s.
The point of every assignment is to learn new things and develop skills. Copying a partner’s work, or splitting an assignment in half so each of you only does part of it, means you gain nothing from it — and since assignments carry much less weight than the examlets and final, that lack of practice will show up on the exams that actually determine your grade.
A better approach: do as much on your own as you can, and talk things over with others when you get stuck. Struggling through your own mistakes until you solve a problem teaches the material far better than being told the answer.


Generative AI policy
You are free to use generative AI tools (ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude, etc.) on Programming Assignments, Homework, and Labs, without restriction — but please briefly cite their use in a code comment where you used them (e.g. // used Claude to help debug this function). If you’re working with a coding agent, you can just ask it to add that disclosure comment for you.
We take this approach because we do not want to spend valuable teaching and learning time trying to detect AI use on take-home work. We believe that you are curious and energetic, and this material is fun to master, so we leave it to you to decide how best to learn it.
That said: the entire point of the PAs, HWs, and Labs is to build understanding you can draw upon independently and fluently. Your understanding, fluency, and expertise will be assessed under invigilated conditions (at ORCA) on the examlets and final exam, which together are worth 80% of your grade. AI will not be available on any CPSC221 assessment in ORCA.
See also UBC’s 10 things UBC students should know about generative AI.


Textbooks
There is no required textbook. Lecture and practice material should be sufficient, but if you’d like a reference:

Discrete Mathematics with Applications (Epp)
Data Abstraction & Problem Solving with C++: Walls and Mirrors (Carrano)

Earlier editions, or textbooks from different authors, work fine too — we’ll be clear about the topics we’re covering so you can find them in any resource. A good C++ reference is a necessity; cppreference.com and learncpp.com are both solid.

title: Syllabus
text:
Note on Course Environment
Some topics discussed in this course may touch on issues that students find personal, sensitive, or challenging. As we explore different perspectives and critically examine ideas, we all share responsibility for maintaining a respectful, inclusive, and supportive learning environment.
Disrespectful, discriminatory, or harmful comments or behaviors related to race, ethnicity, religion, gender identity, sexual orientation, disability, or other personal characteristics will not be tolerated. Our goal is not to win debates or demonstrate superiority, but to learn from one another, engage thoughtfully with complex issues, and develop our understanding through constructive dialogue and collaboration.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Today
Announcements

Labs start next week
HW1 available Monday Sep 14, due Sep 21
Registration for EX1 will be soon!



Where we’re going

The value of an algorithm
The abstraction of running time
What it takes to describe an algorithm precisely

title: CPSC 221
text:
Algorithm analysis
Analysis of an algorithm gives insight into

whether it is correct
how long it runs — time complexity
how much memory it uses — space complexity

All with the aim of making comparisons between different approaches to solving the same problem analytically, not experimentally.

Thirty seconds. This is a framing slide, not a content slide.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Where we stopped

If an algorithm is not correct, is its value 0?



No — and the exceptions are important and worth considering:

approximation — provably close, much faster
heuristics — usually good, no promise
randomized — correct with high probability
restricted inputs — correct on the data you actually have


We spent Wednesday on this. Land the answer and move – do not re-run the discussion, it already happened.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Measuring the value of algorithms
Two algorithms solve the same problem. Which is better?

Use different metrics — time, space most common
Express running time as a (positive) function of input size:

\[T(n): \text{time to complete the operations on data of size } n\]
 
 

The form of that function depends on the structure of the algorithm

Which of these are you willing to wait for?

Anchor: the universe is about 4.4 x 10^17 seconds old.

10^12 s (n^2 at n=10^12) — ~32,000 years. About 5x all of recorded history; back to the Chauvet cave paintings.
10^18 s (2^n at n=100) — ~32 billion years. 2.3x the age of the universe.
10^24 s (n^3 at n=10^12) — ~32 quadrillion years. 2.3 million x the age of the universe.
10^289 s (2^n at n=1000) — 10^271 x the age of the universe. There are only ~10^80 atoms in the observable universe; this exceeds that by 10^209.

If you only use one line: 2^n at n=100 already outruns the universe. Not a million. A hundred.
Small end: 10^-9 s is one nanosecond, and light travels 30 cm in it – Grace Hopper handed out 11.8-inch wires so engineers would stop asking why satellite calls were slow. At 10^-11 s light travels 3 mm.
Two framings if there is time:

The n^3 row is the scary one. 2^n is easy to dismiss as pathological, but n^3 is an innocent triple loop – and at n=10,000 it is already 1 second while n is still at 10^-8.
Faster hardware does not save you. A machine 1000x faster turns 10^289 into 10^286. The exponential eats all of hardware progress and doesn’t notice. That is why this is a math course, not a benchmarking course.

What does it do?

THIS IS THE START OF THE ACTIVITY. Ask it out loud and take two or three answers. You are fishing for something casual and confident – “it finds the key”, “it searches the array”. Do not correct anything; just accept them and move on. The looseness is the setup.
Any C++ mysteries in the code, clear them here – but keep it short.
Do NOT ask “how long does it take?” today. That is Monday’s opening, and asking it now gives away that the description is the hard part.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Somebody said:

“It finds the key.”


And we all nodded.
Now you are going to write that sentence down.

title: CPSC 221
section: Your turn — on your own, in silence
text:
Your turn — on your own, in silence
Describe what this function does.



The rules



Complete sentences. No code, no pseudocode.
Someone who has never seen this function must be able to reimplement it correctly from your words alone.
Give it a name. Fill in the blank.





 

Hold the silence. Five minutes feels long and some will finish in ninety seconds – let them sit with it rather than moving on early. The students who finish fast are usually the ones about to discover they were imprecise.

title: CPSC 221
text:
First: hold up fingers
How many written statements can you see in your group?

I am not asking whether they are any good.
Only whether all three of you have one.

Quick scan of the room. This is a compliance check that costs ten seconds and requires collecting nothing. Groups police themselves.

title: CPSC 221
section: Now read it out loud — all of you, at once
text:
Now read it out loud — all of you, at once
Not one at a time. Everybody, simultaneously, right now.
Nobody is listening to you. That is the point.



Read exactly what you wrote


Do not fix it on the way out of your mouth.



You are going to want to. You will see the gap about half a second before you reach it, and your instinct will be to quietly patch it as you speak.
Resist that. You are reading it so that you can hear it.

Let the whole room read at once – it takes about thirty seconds and the wall of sound is worth having. Two hundred people saying different sentences about the same four lines of code makes the point before anyone discusses anything.
Reading simultaneously does three things a round-robin cannot: it removes all performance anxiety in week 1 among strangers, it guarantees every single student actually does it, and it means no confident voice anchors the group before the others have spoken.
The instruction not to self-repair is the important one. Say it twice. Students patching their own sentences mid-read is automatic and it is exactly what destroys the effect.

title: CPSC 221
section: Did it sound like you expected?
text:
Did it sound like you expected?

Now share them with your group.

Ask this and genuinely wait. A few laughs and groans here are the lesson landing – that is the sound of people hearing their own vagueness.
Do not let them revise before sharing. The group needs the original.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Then: whose is correct?



The test


Could a stranger reimplement this function correctly, from these words alone?



Whose passes?
Any of them?

 

Circulate. Listen for the argument – the groups doing this properly get loud. Silent groups usually accepted the first statement without testing it.
Useful nudge if a group is stuck agreeing: “read me the shortest one, and I’ll tell you how I’d break it.”

title: CPSC 221
section: I will take your words completely literally
text:
I will take your words completely literally

“It finds the key in the list.” → I return true. I found it.
“It returns the position of the key.” → [5, 3, 5], key 5. I return 2. Also a position.
“It returns the index of the key.” → Key isn’t there. I return 0. You didn’t say otherwise.
“It returns where the key is.” → I return a 1-based index. You didn’t say otherwise.
“It searches for the key and returns it.” → I return 5. You said return it.


Use real statements from the room wherever you can – ask for volunteers to read theirs out, and break those instead of these. These are the fallback.
Keep the tone playful. You are being a pedantic genie, not a judge.

title: CPSC 221
section: And the one that catches the careful people
text:
And the one that catches the careful people

“It returns the index of the key, or -1 if the key is not in the list.”



That is a good sentence. It handles absence. It says index.

Let this sit for a beat. Agree with it – genuinely. The room should think this one survived.

title: CPSC 221
section: And the one that catches the careful people
text:
And the one that catches the careful people

“It returns the index of the key, or -1 if the key is not in the list.”



[5, 3, 5], key 5. I return 2.


You never said first.

This is the one that gets the strong students, and it is worth landing carefully – the room should feel that carefulness alone was not sufficient.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Together
(on the board)

Build it live from the room’s own words. Take pieces from different groups so the final sentence visibly belongs to everyone.
A version that survives all the attacks above:

Given a vector of integers arr and an integer q, return the index of the first element of arr equal to q, scanning from index 0 upward. If no element equals q, return -1.

Then the name falls out almost for free: indexOfFirst, firstIndexOf, findFirstIndex. Point out that “find” alone was never enough – a function called find could return a bool, a value, or an iterator.
If somebody has instead transcribed the code line by line (“it loops from 0 to size, and if arr[i] equals q it returns i”), that technically passes the reimplementation test, which makes it a great 90 seconds: it tells you what the code says, never what it is for, and it is no shorter than just reading the code. The giveaway is that a transcription cannot name the function.

title: CPSC 221
text:
What just happened
Twenty minutes ago, almost nobody in this room could write that sentence.
Now almost all of you can.
And notice: I have not taught you anything about linear search today. I have not said one word about how the function works.



You got there by talking to each other.

title: CPSC 221
section: Here is what I could have handed you at the start
text:
Here is what I could have handed you at the start
(live, right now — watch)


It will be correct. It will say first. It will handle absence. It will probably suggest a better name than mine.

title: CPSC 221
section: And you are nodding, because it looks right
text:
And you are nodding, because it looks right


You would have nodded twenty minutes ago too.

Generate this live in front of them if you possibly can – paste the function into whichever tool you like and let the room watch it produce a clean, correct description in about three seconds. Doing it live is far more honest and far more effective than a screenshot, and it removes any suspicion that you cherry-picked.
Do not editorialize while it generates. Let them read it.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Recognizing is not producing
Reading a correct answer and thinking “yes, that’s what I meant” feels exactly like understanding.
It is not the same thing. And from the inside, the two are indistinguishable.
The only way to tell them apart is to try to produce the answer yourself, from nothing — which is what you just spent twenty minutes discovering.
An examlet only ever asks you to produce.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Use the tools
You are allowed to use AI in this course, on homework, assignments, and labs. I mean that.
But what it hands you is a hypothesis until you can produce it yourself.



The check that costs you nothing


Close the laptop. Write the sentence from scratch.
If you can’t, you were holding someone else’s answer.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Before you leave: three words
Your group got somewhere none of you got alone. That happened because somebody in your group refused to accept a vague sentence.
So here is the contract. The three of you agree that from now on, when one of you says something fuzzy, any of the others gets to say:



“Say that more precisely.”


No apology needed. It is not rude. It is the most useful thing you can say to someone who is trying to learn this material.



You will hear me say it all term.

This is the durable takeaway – a shared phrase costs nothing, requires no exchange of anything personal, and gives every student permission to push back on vagueness without it feeling like an attack.
Then start using it yourself, constantly, from Monday on. If they hear it in week 1 and then hear it every week, it stops being an event and becomes how this course talks.

title: CPSC 221
section: And if you want to keep going
text:
And if you want to keep going
Entirely up to you: swap contact info with these two and keep working together.
Piazza, email, Discord, phone —
or nothing at all. No one is checking, and I will never ask.

Say the “or nothing at all” line clearly and move on quickly. In a room this size there will be a few students with real reasons not to hand their number to two people they met twenty minutes ago – and if the whole room is exchanging while you watch, declining becomes conspicuous. Naming the opt-out out loud is what makes it free.
Do not collect anything, do not build a roster, and do not ask next week who is still meeting. The moment there is any follow-up, the opt-out becomes visible again.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Why be in this room
A recording gives you information.
The room gives you feedback.

You just watched a room full of people arrive at an answer that almost none of them had on their own — in twenty minutes, with nothing at stake, and no grade attached.
That is not available anywhere else.

Stop here. Do not add an attendance pitch – the people in the room just lived the argument, and saying it out loud a second time cheapens it.

title: Formatting
text:
In text paragraphs, code is always formatted with a monospace font and surrounded by a box like this. Longer examples of code will be in a separate box.
First line of code
Second line of code
...
In many cases, the output for code in these boxes will be below them.
Replace any placeholder indicated by angular brackets <placeholder> with your own code.
Pressing a KeyKey on the keyboard is formatted like that.

title: C++ Short Course (optional)
text:
All programming assignments in this course use C++. You’ll set up your programming infrastructure and get a brief introduction to the language in your first lab, but if you’d like a more thorough, principled walkthrough of the language beforehand, this optional recorded tutorial series covers the parts of C++ this course actually uses — and the typical “gotchas” that trip people up. What you can do now

Get a head start on C++. Students consistently report that learning C++ is one of the biggest hurdles in this course. We don’t expect prior C++ experience, but some self-study before the term starts will make the labs more comfortable — see the optional C++ Short Course recordings.
Block out your calendar. Put all four course components above on your weekly schedule, and plan blocks of time for PA/HW work.
Check your setup. A significant part of the course is delivered online, so you’ll need a reliable internet connection capable of video. Live class meetings aren’t mandatory, but past students have found them useful. Let us know if you have concerns about your technical setup or access to resources.
Start building study groups. Feel free to use Piazza to coordinate with classmates now.

title: Setup: Tech stack
text: As with any computer science course, CPSC 221 needs a few tools set up before you can start on labs and assignments. Below is the tech stack for this course — the tools and environment you’ll use to write, compile, and submit C++ code.

title: Setup: Tech stack
text:
Hardware
Before starting, ensure that your laptop meets the minimum requirements:

Can connect to networks via a wireless connection.
Has at least 25 GB disk space available.
Has at least 4 GB of RAM (more is recommended).
Uses a 64-bit CPU.
Is at most 6 years old at the start of the course (4 years old or newer is recommended).
Student user has full administrative access to the computer.







Important



If your computer does not meet any of the requirements above, please don’t just drop the course!! Let me know first and we can discuss alternate possibilities so you can still take the course.

title: Setup: Tech stack
text:
Computing environment
All programming assignments and labs in this course use C++, compiled with clang. You submit your .h/.cpp files directly to PrairieLearn, which compiles and tests them for you — but you’ll want a working local (or remote) build to develop and debug against before you submit.

Connect to the department’s remote server
The department provides a shared Linux server for coursework: remote.students.cs.ubc.ca, accessible via SSH with your CWL ID and password (not a separate CS account).
Recommended: VS Code + Remote-SSH

Download VS Code.
Install the Remote - SSH extension (search “SSH - Remote” in the Extensions panel).
Click the new remote-connection icon in the bottom-left corner, choose Add New SSH Host, and enter your-CWL-id@remote.students.cs.ubc.ca.
If prompted for a platform, choose Linux (the remote servers run Linux, regardless of your own OS).
Connect, enter your CWL password, then use the Files Explorer to open a folder — this becomes your working directory on the server.

To skip re-entering your password every time, generate an SSH key and copy it to the server:
ssh-keygen
ssh-copy-id your-CWL-id@remote.students.cs.ubc.ca   # macOS/Linux
(On Windows, use type path\to\id_rsa.pub | ssh your-CWL-id@remote.students.cs.ubc.ca "cat >> .ssh/authorized_keys" instead of ssh-copy-id.)


The command line
You’ll be working at a Linux shell on the remote server. If you’re new to it:
pwd            # print working directory
ls             # list files in the current folder
cd FOLDER      # change into FOLDER; cd .. goes up, cd (no args) goes home
mkdir FOLDER   # create a folder
rm FILE        # delete FILE; rm -r FOLDER deletes a folder and its contents
mv SRC DEST    # move/rename
cp SRC DEST    # copy
make PROGRAM   # build PROGRAM using the rules in a Makefile


Getting lab/assignment files onto the server
Each lab/PA is distributed as a .zip from PrairieLearn. Get it onto the server with either:

VS Code: drag and drop the unzipped folder into the Files Explorer once connected, or
Command line (macOS/Linux): scp your-file.zip your-CWL-id@remote.students.cs.ubc.ca:path/to/folder, then ssh in and unzip your-file.zip.



Compiling and testing
Most labs/PAs include a Makefile. To build:
make
If make fails, read the error message — clang is generally good about pointing at what’s wrong and suggesting a fix. If it succeeds, run the resulting executable directly (e.g. ./lab_intro) to test your work before submitting.
Submission is separate from compiling locally: you upload your source files to the PrairieLearn question, which compiles and grades them independently. A clean local build is a good sign, but the PrairieLearn autograder result is what counts.


C++ references

cplusplus.com and cppreference.com — language/standard library references
Unix and make/Makefile tutorials — the lab starter code builds with make, so a basic understanding of Makefiles will help
If you’re coming from Java: search for “C++ for Java programmers” guides to map concepts you already know onto C++ syntax



C++ short course (optional)
A past offering of this course recorded an optional video series introducing C++ specifically for this course’s needs (classes, pointers, arrays, parameter passing, the “Big 3,” operator overloading). See the C++ Short Course page for the recordings and slides.


More tips and optional readings
The older Computing Environment page has additional background on the department’s servers (it predates the current remote.students.cs.ubc.ca hostname, but the general concepts still apply).

title: Introduction
text:
Summary
Welcome to CPSC 221 — Data Structures and Algorithms! In this course we will learn to design and evaluate programmatic approaches to problem solving. The course has 3 main units. Though they overlap and influence one another, we will address the units in roughly this order:

reasoning about code
classic data structures
graph algorithms

Today’s lesson is an introduction to the context in which we evaluate our code, and the issues we consider when we do so.

title: Introduction
text:
Learning Outcomes
Upon completion of this lesson, students will be able to:

give an overview of the course goals
motivate the tradeoff between order and chaos in data
discuss the metrics used to evaluate an algorithm
explain why running time functions are non-decreasing
